sourcingNote:
Every topic here is factual knowledge (field `sourcing`: "sachwissen"): publicly checkable facts about rules, institutions and procedures in the UK (laws, amounts, who is responsible), written by EnglishAcademy from official sources such as gov.uk and nhs.uk. The UK comes first; short notes compare Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland or the US where they differ.
What is deliberately NOT here: claims about "the British character". Nothing is claimed about people; rules, figures and responsibilities are, and where practice differs by nation, council or person, the topic says so.
Amounts and deadlines change. Every figure carries an "as of" date; if in doubt, the official source is right, not this page.

topics.title: Mr, Ms and first names
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about how people use names and titles in the UK. This is habit, not law: people and workplaces differ, so listen to how others speak.
topics.intro: English has only one word for you. Instead, you choose between a first name and Mr or Ms with a surname. With friends and most colleagues, use the first name.
topics.question: Does your language have a formal and an informal you? When do people use each one?
facts: Use a first name with friends, family and most colleagues: Hello, Sam.
Use Mr, Ms, Mrs or Dr with the surname: Mr Brown, Ms Khan, Dr Lee.
Never use Mr or Ms with only a first name. Say Mr Brown, not Mr John.
Ms is safe for any woman. Use Mrs only if she says she is Mrs.
Many people use first names at work, even with the boss. Listen to what others say.
Not sure? Use Mr, Ms or Dr with the surname. Then ask: What should I call you?

table.label: First name or Mr and Ms?

phrases: Please call me Sam.

Good morning, Mr Brown.

quiz.explain: Ms goes with the surname, not with the first name.

quiz.explain: Sam asked you to use the first name.

quiz.prompt: You do not know if a woman is married. Which title is safe?
quiz.explain: Ms is for any woman. Mrs is only for a woman who uses it.

quiz.prompt: How many words for you does English have?
quiz.explain: The word is you. The formal or informal feeling comes from the names and the words around it.

topics.title: Queuing
topics.sourceNote: General knowledge about common practice in the UK. Queuing is a social rule, not a law, and places differ a little.
topics.intro: In the UK, people queue for buses, shops and many other things. A queue is a line of people who wait. The first person to arrive goes first.
topics.question: Do people queue in your country? What happens at a bus stop?
facts: A queue is a line of people. In the US, people say line.
First come, first served: the person who arrives first goes first.
Stand behind the last person. Do not stand next to them.
Jumping the queue means going in front of other people. This is rude.
At a pub bar there is no line. Wait for your turn and do not wave money.

topics.intro: On Sundays, many shops in the UK open for fewer hours. In England and Wales, a large shop can open for only six hours. Scotland has no limit.
topics.question: When are the shops open in your country? What about on Sundays?
facts: England and Wales: a large shop can open for only 6 hours on Sunday, between 10:00 and 18:00.
Many big supermarkets open from about 10:00 to 16:00 on Sunday.
Small shops, like a corner shop, can open for longer.
Scotland has no Sunday limit. The shop decides its own hours.
On Easter Sunday and Christmas Day, large shops are closed in England and Wales.
Shops at train stations, airports and petrol stations can open for longer.

Taxi or hairdresser: a small tip is nice, but you do not have to.
US restaurant: people expect 15% to 20%.

topics.title: The four nations of the UK
topics.sourceNote: Basic facts about the UK from gov.uk. No population numbers are given here, because they change.
topics.intro: The UK is made up of four nations: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have their own parliament or assembly. Some rules, for example for health and schools, are different in each nation.
topics.question: Is your country one nation or does it have several parts? How are the parts different?
facts: The four nations are England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
The capital cities are London (England and the UK), Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast.
Great Britain is England, Scotland and Wales. The UK is Great Britain plus Northern Ireland.
Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have their own governments: the Scottish Parliament, the Senedd (Welsh Parliament) and the Northern Ireland Assembly.
Devolved means that some decisions are made in each nation, not in London.
The flag of the UK is the Union Jack. Each nation also has its own flag.
In Wales, road signs are in English and Welsh.

topics.title: Bank holidays
topics.sourceNote: Dates and lists from the bank holidays page on gov.uk. The lists are different in each nation and the dates change every year, so check gov.uk for this year. As of 2026.
topics.intro: A bank holiday is a public holiday: many people do not work, and banks and offices close. The UK does not have one list. England and Wales have 8 bank holidays a year, Scotland has 9 and Northern Ireland has 10.
topics.question: Which public holiday from your country do you miss most here?
facts: England and Wales have 8 bank holidays. Scotland has 9. Northern Ireland has 10.
New Year's Day, Good Friday, Christmas Day and Boxing Day are bank holidays in all four nations.
Easter Monday is a bank holiday in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, but not in Scotland.
Scotland also has 2 January and St Andrew's Day (30 November). Northern Ireland also has St Patrick's Day (17 March) and 12 July.
The summer bank holiday is on the last Monday in August in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, but on the first Monday in August in Scotland.
If a bank holiday is on a weekend, another weekday is the substitute day.
Your contract says if you get a day off with pay. Banks and offices are usually closed, and some shops are open.
phrases: Is Monday a bank holiday?

topics.title: Recycling and bin day

topics.intro: In the UK, your local council collects rubbish and recycling from your home. The rules are not the same everywhere: the bin colours, what goes in each bin and the collection day depend on your council. Check your council's website.
topics.question: How do people sort rubbish in your country? Is it more, less or different?
facts: Rules and bin colours depend on your council. Look on its website or in the collection calendar.
Common bins: a general waste bin (often black or grey), a recycling bin (often blue or green) and a small food waste caddy.
Many councils collect different bins in different weeks, so look at the calendar.
Put your bin outside the night before or early on bin day. Check the time for your council.
Empty and rinse bottles, cans and plastic tubs before you recycle them.
A big item, like an old sofa, is bulky waste. Many councils collect it for a fee after you book.
Do not put batteries in your bin. Take them to a shop collection point or to the tip, the local recycling centre.

Call NHS 111 for urgent problems that are not emergencies. Call 999 in an emergency.
Dentists and hairdressers: book by phone or online. Some hairdressers take walk-ins, but booking is safer.

topics.title: First steps: GP, NI number, bank
topics.sourceNote: Public information from gov.uk and nhs.uk. Rules for visas, banks and councils change, so check the official page for your situation (as of 2026).
topics.intro: There is no residence registration in the UK, so you do not have to report your address to the city. Instead, you sort out a few separate things yourself: a GP, a National Insurance number, a bank account and your local council.
topics.question: Do you have to register your address in your home country? What is the first thing people do when they arrive?
facts: There is no central register of residents. Nobody gives you a certificate that says you live at an address.
Register with a GP (a family doctor) near your home. It is free, and you can do it online or at the surgery.
A National Insurance (NI) number is your tax and benefits number. You apply through gov.uk, and you do not need it before you start a job.
Banks usually ask for ID and proof of address, for example a tenancy agreement or a utility bill. Some banks accept other documents, so ask.
Register to vote if you are allowed to. Being on the electoral register also helps with credit checks.
You pay council tax to your local council in England, Scotland and Wales. Full-time students are usually exempt. Northern Ireland has a different system called rates.

topics.title: The NHS: free care, simple rules
topics.sourceNote: Public information from nhs.uk and gov.uk. Charges and the visa health surcharge change, so check the official page (prescription charge as of 2025).
topics.intro: The NHS (National Health Service) gives most health care free at the point of use. This means you do not pay when you see a doctor or go to hospital, because the service is paid for mainly through taxes. You do not choose an insurance company.
topics.question: How do people pay for health care in your country: through taxes, through insurance or privately?
facts: Your first stop is usually your GP. You need to be registered at a surgery to get an appointment.
For a minor problem you can also ask a pharmacist for advice, or call NHS 111 when it is not an emergency.
Call 999 in an emergency. A&E (Accident and Emergency) is for serious injuries and sudden serious illness.
In England a prescription costs £9.90 per item (as of 2025). Prescriptions are free in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and some people in England are exempt.
Dental and eye care often cost money, even in the NHS.
Many people who come to the UK on a visa pay the immigration health surcharge when they apply. After that they can use the NHS in the same way as residents.

topics.title: Renting a flat: deposit and bills
topics.sourceNote: Public information from gov.uk and Shelter (England). Housing law is different in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, and rules change, so check your tenancy agreement (as of 2026).
topics.intro: When you rent a flat in the UK, the monthly rent is only part of the cost. You also pay a deposit at the start, and then council tax and bills such as gas, electricity, water and broadband. Always check what is included before you sign.
topics.question: How do people find a flat in your country, and what do they have to pay at the start?
facts: In England, the Tenant Fees Act 2019 bans most letting fees. A landlord or agent can usually only charge rent, a deposit, a holding deposit and a few other things.
In England the deposit is capped at five weeks' rent if the annual rent is under £50,000.

In England your landlord must put your deposit in a government-approved protection scheme and tell you where it is. You get it back at the end if you pay your rent and leave the flat in good condition.
Council tax depends on your home's band (A to H in England and Scotland, A to I in Wales). Full-time students are usually exempt, and a person who lives alone often gets a discount.
Bills are usually gas, electricity, water, broadband and a TV licence if you watch live TV. Some adverts say 'bills included', which means the rent already covers some of them. Check which ones.
Rules in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are different, for example for deposits and tenancy types.

topics.title: The school system in England
topics.sourceNote: Public information from gov.uk and the Scottish Government. Education is run separately in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, so details differ (as of 2026).
topics.intro: In England children go to primary school and then secondary school, and they stay in education or training until they are 18. Children are grouped by year, from Reception to Year 13. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have their own systems.
topics.question: At what age do children start school in your country, and when do they take their first big exams?
facts: Children start in Reception at age 4 or 5. Primary school covers Reception and Years 1 to 6.
Secondary school is Years 7 to 11. At the end of Year 11, at age 16, students take GCSE exams.
After GCSEs, students stay in education or training until they are 18. Many do A levels in Years 12 and 13, at a sixth form or a college.
State schools are free. Many children wear a school uniform.
Be careful with 'public school'. In England it means a private school that charges fees, not a free state school. 'Private school' and 'independent school' are also used.
Scotland uses different names: primary school (P1 to P7), secondary school (S1 to S6), and exams called Nationals and Highers. Wales and Northern Ireland also differ in details.

topics.intro: In the UK you usually apply for a job with a CV and a cover letter. A UK CV is short and focuses on your skills and experience. Employers must also check that you have the right to work in the UK.
topics.question: What does a CV look like in your country? Is there a photo, a date of birth or a signature?
facts: A UK CV is usually one or two pages long. List your work history starting with your most recent job.
Most UK CVs have no photo, no date of birth and no marital status. Employers should not use these to choose between candidates.
A cover letter (or covering letter) is a short letter that says why you want this job and why you are a good fit. Write a new one for each job.
Employers often ask for two references, for example your last manager. They may contact them only after they have offered you the job.
Employers must check your right to work before you start. If you have a visa, you may give them a 'share code' from gov.uk.
Jobs are advertised on job websites, on company websites and through the government's Find a job service on gov.uk.

topics.title: Apprenticeships and university
topics.sourceNote: Public information from ucas.com and gov.uk. Fees and student finance change every year, so the figures given are for England for the 2025/26 academic year and should be checked on gov.uk (as of 2025).
topics.intro: After school, young people in the UK can either go to university or train in a job as an apprentice. University applications go through a central service called UCAS, while an apprenticeship is a real job with training, and you apply to the employer.
topics.question: In your country, do most people go to university after school, or are there other routes into a career? Which would you choose?
facts: UCAS runs the application system for most UK universities. You can usually apply to up to five courses and write one personal statement that explains why you want to study the subject.
The main UCAS deadline for most courses is in January. Some courses, such as medicine, and applications to Oxford and Cambridge, have an earlier deadline in October. Check ucas.com for the dates.

In England, universities can charge tuition fees of up to £9,535 a year for home students in 2025/26 (as of 2025). Student loans can cover the fees, and graduates repay them from their salary once they earn above a threshold.
Scottish students who study at a Scottish university generally pay no tuition fees. Students from elsewhere in the UK usually do.
An apprenticeship combines paid work with training. You earn a wage, your employer trains you, and you study part of the time with a college or a training provider.
Apprenticeships have levels. Level 2 is roughly the standard of GCSEs, level 3 of A levels, and higher and degree apprenticeships (levels 4 to 7) can lead to a degree.

topics.title: Notice, resigning and references
topics.sourceNote: Public information from gov.uk and Acas. Employment law is changing under the Employment Rights Act 2025, so check gov.uk or Acas for the rules that apply now (as of 2026).
topics.intro: When you leave a job in the UK, or an employer ends your contract, a period of notice usually applies. The length depends on your contract and on how long you have worked there. In practice, most people hand in a short resignation letter and ask for a reference.
topics.question: How much notice do employees give in your country, and is the rule set by law or by the contract?
facts: The statutory minimum notice from an employer is one week if you have worked there for at least one month, then one week for each full year of service, up to a maximum of 12 weeks.
An employee has to give at least one week's notice after one month of service, unless the contract asks for more. Many contracts say one month, so read yours carefully.
A resignation letter is short and polite. It states your last day and does not have to give your reasons.
When you leave, your employer gives you a P45. It shows your pay and tax so far, and your next employer may ask for it.
References are usually factual: dates of employment and job title, and sometimes more. Employers are not required to give a reference in most cases, but they must make sure it is accurate.
Unfair dismissal protection generally starts after two years of service, but the Employment Rights Act 2025 brings changes in stages, so check the current rules before you rely on this.

My last day will be the thirty-first of March.

topics.title: The BBC and the TV licence
topics.sourceNote: Public information from tvlicensing.co.uk and the BBC (bbc.co.uk). The licence fee is reviewed every year, and the BBC's charter is due for renewal, so check the current figure (licence fee as of 2025).
topics.intro: The BBC is the UK's public broadcaster, and it is paid for mainly by a licence fee rather than by adverts. Households that watch live television or use BBC iPlayer must buy a TV licence, and many people argue about whether this is fair.
topics.question: Do you think everyone should pay for public broadcasting, or only the people who use it? Why?
facts: The TV licence costs £174.50 a year for a standard colour licence (as of 2025). The amount changes, so check tvlicensing.co.uk.
You need a licence to watch or record live TV on any channel, and to watch or download programmes on BBC iPlayer.
A licence covers one address (per household), not each person. In shared flats with separate tenancy agreements, each tenant may need their own, so check the rules.
BBC television and radio in the UK have no adverts. The BBC is funded mainly by the licence fee, and also earns money from commercial activities abroad.
The BBC works under a Royal Charter, a document that sets out its purpose and how it is run. The current charter runs until the end of 2027 (as of 2025).
Streaming on Netflix or watching YouTube on demand does not need a licence on its own.

pros: The BBC does not depend on advertisers or on a single owner
Everyone pays a small amount, so a wide range of programmes can be made for all audiences
Programmes without commercial value, such as news, children's TV and local radio, can be funded
A public broadcaster can be held accountable to the public through its charter
cons: People who rarely watch the BBC still have to pay if they watch live TV
The fee is a flat charge, so it is the same for rich and poor households
Viewing habits are moving to streaming, so some people question the link to a TV set
Critics say a subscription or adverts would be fairer and more flexible

Universities have student societies, and many workplaces have social or sports clubs.
Charity shops sell second-hand clothes, books and household items, and the money goes to a charity. They are often staffed by volunteers and are a popular place to find bargains.

topics.title: Devolution: who decides what in the UK
topics.sourceNote: Publicly checkable general knowledge (gov.uk, parliament.uk; the devolution Acts for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland). The list of devolved powers has been widened several times, so check the current position as of 2026.
topics.intro: Ask who runs education in the UK and the honest answer is: it depends where you are. Since 1999 Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have had their own elected bodies with power over many everyday matters, while the UK Parliament at Westminster keeps the rest. The result is a union that is governed in four different ways.
topics.question: Is your country governed from the centre, or do regions have their own parliaments? Who decides about schools and hospitals there?
facts: Westminster remains sovereign: the UK Parliament passed the devolution Acts and could, in legal theory, change or repeal them. In practice, by convention, it does not legislate on devolved matters without the consent of the devolved legislature.

Scotland has the Scottish Parliament (Holyrood), Wales has the Senedd (the Welsh Parliament), and Northern Ireland has the Assembly, which sits at Stormont in Belfast and is based on power-sharing between the main communities. The Assembly has been suspended at times, most recently from 2022 until early 2024.

Powers are either reserved or devolved. Reserved matters stay with Westminster, for example defence, foreign policy, immigration and most of the tax and benefits system. Devolved matters, such as health, education and much of transport, are decided locally, although the exact list differs between the three nations.

England has no parliament or government of its own. English health, education and housing policy is made by the UK government and Parliament, so MPs from Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish seats can vote on laws that apply only in England. People call this the 'English question'.

Local government is a further layer. In England, councils run services such as social care, planning, libraries and bin collection, and some city regions have a directly elected metro mayor, for example in Greater Manchester and the West Midlands, with powers that vary from deal to deal.

Because health and education are devolved, everyday rules differ across the UK. A prescription is free in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland but not in England (with exemptions), and the school systems are separate.

topics.title: National Insurance and the welfare state
topics.sourceNote: Publicly checkable general knowledge (gov.uk: National Insurance, State Pension, Universal Credit, workplace pensions). Rates and thresholds change, often each April, so no rates are given here; check gov.uk for the figures as of 2026.
topics.intro: National Insurance sounds like an insurance scheme, but in practice it works largely as a tax that also builds your entitlement to certain benefits. The UK welfare state mixes benefits you earn through contributions with benefits that depend on your income and circumstances. The NHS, often assumed to be funded by National Insurance, is paid for mainly from general taxation.
topics.question: How are pensions, sickness pay and healthcare financed in your country? Do you pay into separate funds?
facts: Most employees and the self-employed pay National Insurance contributions once their earnings pass a threshold. Your record of 'qualifying years' decides what contribution-based benefits you can claim.

For the full new State Pension you need 35 qualifying years on your National Insurance record, and at least 10 qualifying years to get any State Pension at all. Years can also be credited, for example for some periods of caring or receiving certain benefits.

The NHS is funded mainly from general taxation, with National Insurance contributing only part of the total. There is no separate health insurance contribution, and most NHS services are free at the point of use.

Universal Credit is the main working-age benefit. It replaced six older benefits and is paid monthly in a single payment, with the amount depending on income, savings, housing costs and family circumstances rather than on contributions.
Statutory Sick Pay is paid by your employer for a limited period (up to 28 weeks) if you are too ill to work and meet the conditions. Many employers pay more under their own sick pay schemes.

Under automatic enrolment, employers must put eligible workers into a workplace pension and pay in too. Workers can opt out, and the rules on age and earnings thresholds are set by the government and can be revised.

topics.title: General elections and first past the post
topics.sourceNote: Publicly checkable general knowledge (parliament.uk, gov.uk, the Electoral Commission). Voting ages, systems and ID rules can change, so check the position as of 2026 before relying on any detail.
topics.intro: In a UK general election you cast a single vote for one candidate in your local constituency, and you do not vote for the Prime Minister at all. The candidate with the most votes wins the seat, even without a majority, and the party that can command a majority in the House of Commons forms the government. This system is called first past the post.
topics.question: How are MPs or representatives elected in your country: by majority, by proportion of votes, or a mixture? What do you think of it?
facts: The UK is divided into 650 constituencies, each electing one Member of Parliament (MP) to the House of Commons. Whoever gets the most votes in a constituency wins the seat; an absolute majority is not required and there is no second round.

A general election must be held at least every five years. The Prime Minister no longer chooses the date freely in the way some other systems allow: the law sets the maximum term, and Parliament is dissolved by the monarch on the Prime Minister's request.
The Prime Minister is not elected directly. By convention, the monarch appoints the person who is best placed to command a majority in the Commons, usually the leader of the largest party.
The voting age for UK general elections is 18. It is already 16 for elections to the Scottish Parliament and the Senedd. The government has announced plans to lower it to 16 for UK elections as well.

Other systems are used elsewhere in the UK. Holyrood uses the additional member system, which combines constituency seats with regional list seats. The Senedd is moving to a closed list system from 2026, and the Northern Ireland Assembly is elected by the single transferable vote (STV).

Photo ID is required at polling stations for UK general elections in Great Britain, and has been since 2023. Northern Ireland has had its own photo ID rule since 2003. Anyone without suitable ID can apply for a free voter authority certificate.
phrases: The winner takes the seat on a simple plurality of votes.
It's arguably unfair that seats don't match the share of the vote.
In a safe seat, many voters feel their vote hardly makes a difference.
I'd concede that it tends to produce stable governments, though.
Some voters vote tactically rather than for their first choice.

topics.title: Remembrance: poppies, silence and memorials
topics.sourceNote: Publicly checkable general knowledge (britishlegion.org.uk, gov.uk, Royal British Legion and Imperial War Museums materials). Dates and customs are stable, but check the Legion's website for each year's appeal as of 2026.
topics.intro: Every November, much of the UK pauses to remember those who died in war. People wear red paper poppies from late October, and there are ceremonies at war memorials in nearly every town and village. Remembrance in the UK is a mixture of national ceremony, local tradition and personal choice.
topics.question: How does your country remember people who died in war? Are there particular days, symbols or ceremonies?
facts: Armistice Day is on 11 November, marking the end of fighting in the First World War in 1918. A two-minute silence is observed at 11 am, the time the armistice took effect.

Remembrance Sunday falls on the second Sunday in November. The main national service takes place at the Cenotaph in Whitehall, London, where wreaths are laid and a two-minute silence is observed at 11 am. It commemorates those who died in both world wars and in later conflicts.

The red poppy is the symbol of the Royal British Legion's annual Poppy Appeal, which raises money for serving and former members of the armed forces and their families. The flower is linked to the poppies that grew on First World War battlefields. In Scotland, the appeal is run by Poppy Scotland.
War memorials stand in most towns and villages, often listing local names from the First and Second World Wars. Many communities hold their own short ceremony at the memorial on Remembrance Sunday.

Wearing a poppy is a personal choice. Some people choose a white poppy, sold by the Peace Pledge Union, to stand for peace and a rejection of war, and some choose not to wear any symbol. Views on the meaning of remembrance differ, and respect for others' choices is the general expectation.
On the day itself, the silence is widely observed in public places: shops, stations, sports events and workplaces often stop for two minutes, and broadcasters mark it too.
phrases: We observed the two minutes' silence at the war memorial.
Wearing a poppy is entirely a matter of personal choice.
It's a time to pay one's respects to those who gave their lives.
I hope you don't mind my asking what the poppy stands for.
Remembrance means rather different things to different people.

quiz.explain: Armistice Day itself is on 11 November, whatever the day of the week.

topics.title: The uncodified constitution and the Supreme Court
topics.sourceNote: Publicly checkable general knowledge (parliament.uk, supremecourt.uk, legislation.gov.uk). The constitution evolves through new Acts and court judgments, so check the position as of 2026 for anything recent.
topics.intro: The United Kingdom has no single written document called 'the Constitution'. Its rules are spread across Acts of Parliament, court decisions and unwritten conventions, which is why lawyers call it uncodified. This makes the system flexible, but it also means that what counts as 'constitutional' is sometimes argued over.
topics.question: Does your country have a written constitution? Who can strike down a law that breaks it?
facts: The main sources are statutes, the common law and constitutional conventions. Statutes include Magna Carta of 1215, of which only a few clauses are still in force, the Bill of Rights of 1689, the Acts of Union and the Human Rights Act 1998.

Parliamentary sovereignty is the central principle: Parliament can make or unmake any law, and no earlier Parliament can bind a later one. Courts therefore apply Acts of Parliament rather than overturning them.

The Human Rights Act 1998 brought the rights of the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law. If a court finds an Act incompatible with them, it can issue a declaration of incompatibility, but the Act stays in force until Parliament decides what to do.

Conventions are rules of political practice that are not enforced as law. For example, the monarch gives royal assent to legislation passed by Parliament, and a Prime Minister is expected to have the confidence of the House of Commons.

The Supreme Court of the United Kingdom began work in October 2009. Before that, the highest court of appeal was a committee of the House of Lords. It has twelve justices and hears the most important appeals on points of law.

In 2019, in R (Miller) v The Prime Minister, the Supreme Court held that the advice to prorogue Parliament was unlawful because it stopped Parliament doing its constitutional job without reasonable justification. This case shows courts reviewing the exercise of government power, not striking down an Act.

phrases: Strictly speaking, there is no single codified constitution.
That's a matter of convention rather than law.
Parliament is sovereign, so the courts can't strike down an Act.

quiz.prompt: Why is the UK constitution called 'uncodified'?
options: It is not collected in one single written document
It has never been written down at all
quiz.answer: It is not collected in one single written document
quiz.explain: Parts of it are written, in statutes and judgments; other parts are conventions.

quiz.explain: Parliament then decides whether to change the law.

quiz.answer: That the prorogation of Parliament was unlawful

topics.title: Trade unions and workers' rights
topics.sourceNote: Publicly checkable general knowledge (gov.uk, Acas, the Department for Business and Trade's trade union statistics, the TUC). Pay rates and employment law change often, and the Employment Rights Act 2025 is being phased in, so check the position as of 2026 on gov.uk.
topics.intro: In the UK, workers' rights come mainly from legislation and from individual employment contracts, with trade unions acting as a collective voice for those who choose to join. Union membership is voluntary, and there is no general legal requirement for a works council in every larger workplace. How much influence workers have therefore varies a great deal between sectors.
topics.question: Do workers in your country usually belong to trade unions? Who negotiates pay, the union or the individual?
facts: The Trades Union Congress (TUC) is the main federation of unions in Britain and was founded in 1868. Individual unions represent workers in a trade, profession or employer, and some are among the largest organisations in the country.

Government statistics from the Department for Business and Trade put union membership at around a fifth of employees, roughly 22 % (figures published for 2024). Membership is much higher in the public sector than in private firms.

Collective bargaining with the employer is much less widespread than in some other countries, and a worker's pay is more often set by their individual contract. Where an employer recognises a union, it negotiates on behalf of its members.

Strikes are lawful only if the union follows strict rules, including a ballot of members and notice to the employer. Workers on strike are not automatically protected from every consequence, so legal details matter.

The National Minimum Wage and National Living Wage set a legal floor for pay. As of April 2025 the National Living Wage was £12.21 an hour for workers aged 21 and over; rates are reviewed every year, so check gov.uk for the current figure.

Acas, the Advisory, Conciliation and Arbitration Service, gives free advice and helps resolve disputes. Claims about issues such as unfair dismissal can go to an employment tribunal, and the process normally starts with early conciliation through Acas. The Employment Rights Act 2025 is being phased in and changes a number of rules, so check which provisions apply now.
